intro: These five verbs each have one concrete core, and most of their partners are that core stretched. かける hangs, pours or aims one thing over or at another; つける attaches something so it stays on, or switches something on; 出す moves something out from you into the world; 取る takes something into your hands and makes it yours; 引く pulls something towards you or draws it out. English uses take, make, have, put and catch for all of these, so the English verb is a poor guide: learn each noun with its verb as one unit, and when you hesitate, ask which core picture the noun fits.

skills.rule: Phone calls, glasses, locks, music, salt poured over food, time spent, trouble caused and a word to someone all take かける: something is hung on, spread over or aimed at a target.
skills.explain:
かける (掛ける) is to hang or lay one thing over another. Literally: 眼鏡をかける (put on or wear glasses: they hang on your ears), 鍵をかける (lock: the bolt goes across), 塩をかける (sprinkle salt over food), ソースをかける.

It also means aiming something at a target: 電話をかける (make a phone call; 電話する is also fine), 声をかける (speak to someone, call out to them), 迷惑をかける (cause someone trouble), 音楽をかける (put on music, play a song or CD). And 時間をかける / お金をかける is to spend time or money on something on purpose.

The person affected takes に: 友達に電話をかける, 先生に声をかける, 人に迷惑をかける. The intransitive partner is かかる: 時間がかかる (it takes time; nobody chooses to spend it), 鍵がかかっている (it is locked). Glasses take かける, but a hat is かぶる and a watch or tie is する.
patterns: [person] に 電話 / 声 / 迷惑 を かける
[food] に 塩 / ソース を かける
眼鏡 / 鍵 / 音楽 を かける
[task] に 時間 / お金 を かける

examples.jp: 母[はは]に電話[でんわ]を{かけました}。
examples.en: I phoned my mother.

examples.jp: 父[ちち]は新聞[しんぶん]を読[よ]むとき、眼鏡[めがね]を{かけます}。
examples.en: My father puts on his glasses when he reads the newspaper.

examples.jp: 家[いえ]を出[で]る前[まえ]に、鍵[かぎ]を{かけて}ください。
examples.en: Please lock the door before you leave the house.

examples.jp: 目玉焼[めだまや]きに塩[しお]を少[すこ]し{かけて}食[た]べます。
examples.en: I sprinkle a little salt on my fried egg before eating it.

examples.jp: この料理[りょうり]は時間[じかん]を{かけて}作[つく]りました。
examples.en: I took my time making this dish.

examples.jp: 皆[みな]さんにご迷惑[めいわく]を{おかけして}、申[もう]し訳[わけ]ありません。
examples.en: I am very sorry to have caused you all trouble.

contrast.note: Music and devices differ: 音楽をかける is putting on a song, but テレビ / ラジオをつける is switching the set on. Salt poured over food is 塩をかける; seasoning a dish in general is 味をつける.
電話をかける and 電話する both mean to phone. But many other worn items take する (時計をする, ネクタイをする, マスクをする), and hats take かぶる.
時間がかかる: the job takes time, no chooser. 時間をかける: someone deliberately spends time on it. The same split for お金がかかる / お金をかける.

mistakes.bad: 友達[ともだち]に迷惑[めいわく]を{しました}。
mistakes.good: 友達[ともだち]に迷惑[めいわく]を{かけました}。
mistakes.note: Trouble you cause someone is 迷惑をかける. 迷惑する means you are the one who is bothered.

mistakes.bad: 駅[えき]で先生[せんせい]に声[こえ]を{出[だ]しました}。
mistakes.good: 駅[えき]で先生[せんせい]に声[こえ]を{かけました}。
mistakes.note: Speaking to a person is 声をかける, aimed at someone with に. 声を出す only means making a sound.

mistakes.bad: 腕時計[うでどけい]を{かけて}います。
mistakes.good: 腕時計[うでどけい]を{して}います。
mistakes.note: Glasses hang on your face, so かける; a wristwatch is worn with する.

skills.tip: Picture the noun going over or at a target: glasses over the ears, salt over food, the bolt across the door, a call or a word aimed at a person. Draped or aimed means かける.

skills.rule: When something is attached so it stays (a name, flavour, ointment, strength, entries in a diary, your attention) or a device is switched on, use つける.
skills.explain:
つける (付ける) is to attach one thing firmly to another. 名前をつける is to give something a name (猫に名前をつける); 味をつける is to season (醤油で味をつける); 薬をつける is to put cream or ointment on the skin; 日記をつける is to keep a diary, adding an entry day by day; 力をつける is to build up strength or skill so that it stays with you. 気をつける, literally attaching your attention, is to be careful: 車に気をつけて.

Switching on is also つける: 電気 / テレビ / エアコンをつける. The opposite is 消す, and the intransitive partner is つく: 電気がつく (the light comes on).

Medicine you swallow is 飲む, never つける or 取る; つける is only for what goes on the skin. A diary can also be 書く, but keeping one as a habit is つける. 気をつける (take care) is not 気がつく (notice) or 気にする (worry about).
patterns: [thing] に 名前 / 味 / 薬 を つける
電気 / テレビ / エアコン を つける
[danger] に 気 を つける
日記 / 力 を つける

examples.jp: 部屋[へや]が暗[くら]いので、電気[でんき]を{つけました}。
examples.en: The room was dark, so I turned on the light.

examples.jp: 車[くるま]に気[き]を{つけて}ね。
examples.en: Watch out for cars.

examples.jp: 新[あたら]しい猫[ねこ]に名前[なまえ]を{つけました}。
examples.en: I gave the new cat a name.

examples.jp: 毎晩[まいばん]、日記[にっき]を{つけて}います。
examples.en: I keep a diary, writing in it every night.

examples.jp: 傷[きず]にこの薬[くすり]を{つけて}ください。
examples.en: Please put this ointment on the cut.

examples.jp: 毎日[まいにち]練習[れんしゅう]して、日本語[にほんご]の力[ちから]を{つけたい}です。
examples.en: I want to build up my Japanese by practising every day.

contrast.note: Both put something on something. かける pours or drapes it over (塩をかける, ソースをかける); つける attaches it so it stays (味をつける, 薬をつける). Glasses are かける.
入れる puts something inside: コーヒーに砂糖を入れる, スイッチを入れる (flip the switch). For lights and the TV the everyday verb is つける.
力をつける is to build ability up over time; 力を出す is to exert the strength you have right now (全力を出す).

mistakes.bad: 風邪[かぜ]の薬[くすり]を{つけました}。
mistakes.good: 風邪[かぜ]の薬[くすり]を{飲[の]みました}。
mistakes.note: Pills and syrup are swallowed: 飲む. つける is only for creams put on the skin.

mistakes.bad: 道[みち]が滑[すべ]るから、気[き]を{して}ください。
mistakes.good: 道[みち]が滑[すべ]るから、気[き]を{つけて}ください。
mistakes.note: Be careful is the fixed pair 気をつける. 気にする means to worry about something.

skills.tip: Does it stick and stay on (a name, a flavour, cream, a skill, your attention), or does it come on (a light)? Then it is つける.

skills.rule: When something goes out from you into the world (a letter into the post, homework to the teacher, your voice, money, rubbish, a conclusion, your energy), use 出す.
skills.explain:
出す is to put or send something out. 手紙を出す is to post a letter; 宿題を出す is to hand in homework, or, said of a teacher, to set it; ごみを出す is to put the rubbish out for collection; お金を出す is to pay or put money towards something (半分出す, pay half).

It also brings out what is inside you: 声を出す (make a sound, speak up: 大きな声を出す), 元気を出す (cheer up: 元気を出して is a common word of encouragement), 結論を出す (reach and state a conclusion), 力を出す (exert your strength).

送る stresses sending something to a person (メールを送る, 荷物を送る); posting a letter is normally 出す. Speaking to someone is 声をかける, not 声を出す. The intransitive partner is 出る: 結論が出た (a conclusion was reached), 宿題が出た (homework was set).
patterns: [person] に 手紙 / 宿題 を 出す
ごみ / お金 を 出す
声 / 元気 / 結論 を 出す

examples.jp: 郵便局[ゆうびんきょく]で手紙[てがみ]を{出[だ]しました}。
examples.en: I posted a letter at the post office.

examples.jp: 宿題[しゅくだい]は金曜日[きんようび]までに{出[だ]して}ください。
examples.en: Please hand in your homework by Friday.

examples.jp: 燃[も]えるごみは月曜日[げつようび]の朝[あさ]に{出[だ]します}。
examples.en: Burnable rubbish goes out on Monday morning.

examples.jp: 図書館[としょかん]では大[おお]きい声[こえ]を{出[だ]さないで}ください。
examples.en: Please do not speak loudly in the library.

examples.jp: 元気[げんき]を{出[だ]して}。また頑張[がんば]ろう。
examples.en: Cheer up. Let's try again.

examples.jp: 長[なが]い会議[かいぎ]のあと、やっと結論[けつろん]を{出[だ]しました}。
examples.en: After a long meeting we finally reached a conclusion.

contrast.note: 送る is sending to a person or address: メールを送る, 荷物を送る. 手紙を出す is the everyday way to say you posted a letter.
声を出す is producing sound (shout, read aloud, speak up). 声をかける is addressing a person, with に.
上げる moves something up: 手を上げる (raise your hand), 値段を上げる. 出す moves it out: 手を出す is to reach out for something, or to meddle.

mistakes.bad: 先生[せんせい]に宿題[しゅくだい]を{あげました}。
mistakes.good: 先生[せんせい]に宿題[しゅくだい]を{出[だ]しました}。
mistakes.note: Homework is handed in with 出す. あげる would make it a present.

mistakes.bad: 歌[うた]うときは、もっと声[こえ]を{かけて}ください。
mistakes.good: 歌[うた]うときは、もっと声[こえ]を{出[だ]して}ください。
mistakes.note: Making more sound is 声を出す. 声をかける means speaking to someone.

skills.tip: Out of your hands or out of your body into the world: the post box, the teacher's desk, the collection point, the air. Outward means 出す.

skills.rule: When you take something into your possession or control (time off, a score, notes, a booking, contact, responsibility, years of age, a meal), use 取る.
skills.explain:
取る is to take something in your hand, and by extension to get or secure it. 休みを取る is to take time off; 点を取る is to score or get a mark; メモを取る is to take notes; 予約を取る is to get a booking (予約する means the same); 連絡を取る is to get in touch, with と (友達と連絡を取る); 責任を取る is to take responsibility for a failure, usually by resigning or making amends.

Two uses English speakers do not expect: 年を取る is to grow old, and 食事を取る is to have a meal, a slightly formal phrase used in health advice and announcements. In conversation say 食事をする or 食べる.

取る is not English take everywhere. Medicine is 飲む, a photo is 撮る (same sound, different kanji), a train is 乗る, a shower is 浴びる, and the time a job needs is かかる. 持つ means hold or have, not get: 傘を持つ.
patterns: 休み / 点 / メモ / 予約 を 取る
[person] と 連絡 を 取る
責任 / 年 を 取る
食事 を 取る (formal)

examples.jp: 来週[らいしゅう]、三日間[みっかかん]休[やす]みを{取[と]ります}。
examples.en: I am taking three days off next week.

examples.jp: 先生[せんせい]の話[はなし]を聞[き]きながら、メモを{取[と]りました}。
examples.en: I took notes while listening to the teacher.

examples.jp: 数学[すうがく]のテストでいい点[てん]を{取[と]りました}。
examples.en: I got a good mark in the maths test.

examples.jp: 七時[しちじ]でレストランの予約[よやく]を{取[と]りました}。
examples.en: I booked a table at the restaurant for seven.

examples.jp: 祖父[そふ]は年[とし]を{取[と]って}、あまり歩[ある]けなくなりました。
examples.en: My grandfather has grown old and can't walk much any more.

examples.jp: 社長[しゃちょう]が事故[じこ]の責任[せきにん]を{取[と]って}辞[や]めました。
examples.en: The company president took responsibility for the accident and resigned.

contrast.note: Some nouns take either: 予約する / 予約を取る, 食事する / 食事を取る, 連絡する / 連絡を取る. 年, 点 and 責任 need 取る (メモする is fine, but メモを取る is the usual phrase with を), and 休みをする is not Japanese (use 休む or 休みを取る).
責任を持つ is being in charge of something going forward; 責任を取る is accepting the blame after something went wrong. 持つ holds, 取る takes.
写真を撮る is the same sound with a different kanji. Medicine is always 飲む, even when English says take.

mistakes.bad: 一週間[いっしゅうかん]休[やす]みを{して}、旅行[りょこう]します。
mistakes.good: 一週間[いっしゅうかん]休[やす]みを{取[と]って}、旅行[りょこう]します。
mistakes.note: Taking leave is 休みを取る, or simply 休む.

mistakes.bad: 風邪[かぜ]なので、薬[くすり]を{取[と]って}寝[ね]ました。
mistakes.good: 風邪[かぜ]なので、薬[くすり]を{飲[の]んで}寝[ね]ました。
mistakes.note: Taking medicine is 飲む. 薬を取る only means picking up the box.

mistakes.bad: 失敗[しっぱい]の責任[せきにん]を{持[も]ちました}。
mistakes.good: 失敗[しっぱい]の責任[せきにん]を{取[と]りました}。
mistakes.note: Accepting the blame for a failure is 責任を取る.

skills.tip: Can you picture grabbing it and making it yours: leave, points, notes, a booking, the blame, more years? Then 取る. If you swallow it, ride it or photograph it, it is another verb.

skills.rule: When something is pulled towards you or drawn out (a cold you catch, a word you look up, a line, a lot, someone's interest, a hand you lead), use 引く.
skills.explain:
引く is to pull. 線を引く is to draw a line (you pull the pen across); くじを引く is to draw a lot or a raffle ticket; 辞書を引く is to look a word up in a dictionary; 手を引く is to lead someone by the hand (子どもの手を引く), and figuratively to pull out of something (計画から手を引く).

風邪を引く (often written 風邪をひく) is to catch a cold. It is the fixed verb: 風邪を取る is wrong. Most other illnesses take にかかる: インフルエンザにかかる.

興味を引く is to attract interest, and its subject is the interesting thing: そのニュースは多くの人の興味を引いた. When you are the one who is interested, the verb is 持つ: 日本の歴史に興味を持つ. Getting this direction wrong is the commonest error with 引く.
patterns: 風邪 を 引く
辞書 を 引く
[place] に 線 を 引く
くじ を 引く
[thing] が [person] の 興味 を 引く
[person] の 手 を 引く

examples.jp: 冬[ふゆ]はよく風邪[かぜ]を{引[ひ]きます}。
examples.en: I often catch colds in winter.

examples.jp: 分[わ]からない言葉[ことば]は辞書[じしょ]を{引[ひ]いて}調[しら]べます。
examples.en: I look up words I don't know in the dictionary.

examples.jp: 大事[だいじ]なところに線[せん]を{引[ひ]いて}ください。
examples.en: Please underline the important parts.

examples.jp: お祭[まつ]りでくじを{引[ひ]いたら}、一等[いっとう]が当[あ]たりました。
examples.en: I drew a lottery ticket at the festival and won first prize.

examples.jp: 母親[ははおや]が子[こ]どもの手[て]を{引[ひ]いて}歩[ある]いています。
examples.en: A mother is walking along leading her child by the hand.

examples.jp: その新[あたら]しいゲームは若[わか]い人[ひと]の興味[きょうみ]を{引[ひ]きました}。
examples.en: The new game caught the interest of young people.

contrast.note: 興味を持つ: I am interested (in に). 興味を引く: something attracts someone's interest (the interesting thing is the subject).
A cold is 風邪を引く. Most other illnesses are [illness] にかかる: 病気にかかる, インフルエンザにかかる.
辞書を引く is the set phrase for looking a word up. 辞書で調べる also works, with で; 辞書を見る is loose and casual.

mistakes.bad: 昨日[きのう]から風邪[かぜ]を{取[と]って}います。
mistakes.good: 昨日[きのう]から風邪[かぜ]を{引[ひ]いて}います。
mistakes.note: Catching or having a cold is 風邪を引く; 取る never works here.

mistakes.bad: 私[わたし]は日本[にほん]の歌[うた]に興味[きょうみ]を{引[ひ]いて}います。
mistakes.good: 私[わたし]は日本[にほん]の歌[うた]に興味[きょうみ]を{持[も]って}います。
mistakes.note: You hold an interest (持つ); the thing pulls it towards itself (引く).

skills.tip: Pull: a pen across paper, a ticket out of a box, a child by the hand, a cold into your body, people's interest towards a thing. Pulling means 引く.
